articles.text: Piedmont’s best bird impersonators are currently making last minute tweaks and squeaks to their bird calls for the 55th annual Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest on Friday, March 29, at 7:00 p.m. This year’s contest at the Alan Harvey Theater continues the wacky tradition of pageantry and whimsy begun a half century ago by former Piedmont High School biology teacher Leonard Waxdeck. Bird calls scheduled to be heard include the Cooper’s Hawk, Ruddy Duck, Blakiston’s Fish Eagle, the Eurasian Owl, Clark’s Nutcracker, Bonaparte’s Gull, Cliff Swallow, and the rather “bloodthirsty” Montezuma Quail. A panel of judges will include PHS grad Alex Hirsch, a former contest winner and creator of the hit Disney animation series Gravity Falls. This year’s ornithology judge is PHS alum Yossi Fendel, with PHS math teacher Auban Willats as an additional judge. Senior Daniel Banin will serve as master of ceremonies. Fourteen entries will try to impress the judges and the PHS senior Kira Pan’s poster design.

articles.text: Editor: I am a Piedmont resident living on Maxwelton Road, I have attended two of the preceding presentations regarding the four options for the plan that is required by the State of California. I was unable to attend city Council meeting last Monday and I’m writing to express my opinions regarding in plan. My conversations with city planning staff, specifically Mr. Kevin Jackson has brought to my attention that the state of California did not take into consideration the amount of available open space in each city when the number of units that they are requiring to be built are calculated. I think the housing problem in California and in the San Francisco Bay area is regional and that should be addressed on a one plan fits all formula. It’s obvious that we are going to have to SACRIFICE the very precious and limited parks and the limited existing recreational field that we have in the City of Piedmont. The population of the nine counties in the San Francisco Bay Aare has decreased in recent years by approximately 250,000 according to US census data. We have seen tremendous number of new housing units being built in our neighboring cities that did not require the sacrifice of green spaces and parks. There is an abundance of new housing going up and having recently been built in Oakland, Emeryville, Berkeley, Albany El Cerrito and Richmond, none of which required the loss of Green space in those cities. The Moraga Canyon and the Blair Park side are the lowest hanging fruit. I think Plan No. 1, putting all of the units on the Blair Park site, is the worst of all of the bad options. The density of the number of units in that small area [would create] additional traffic on Moraga Road which is already often very congested. I urge the Piedmont City Council to try to resist implementing this ill-conceived state mandated project by whatever means necessary. It should be put off in whatever manner possible. It’s possible and very likely that there will be a change in the political climate or the demographics of our area that will prove it to have been a mistake to build. –Alan R. articles.text: Early Bird discounts end this week With four weeks remaining until Piedmont Food Fest, attendees are starting to scope out the vast food & entertainment options, sign up to volunteer, and visit the website to register for the free event as well as grab Early Bird discounts on KidZone passes, Premium Beer & Wine Tastings, and event merch. Since its premiere in April 2022 and return last year, Piedmont Food Fest has attracted over 3000 attendees who’ve enjoyed the mix of multicultural food, drink, and performances curated from all around the Bay Area. From quesabirrias to pork belly buns to hot chicken sandwiches, from boba milk tea to gourmet lemonade, Food Festers have grown accustomed to discovering something delicious and new at this newest Piedmont tradition. This year’s lineup of food vendors will include fan favorites such as Robert Dorsey Catering, The Chairman, La Santa Torta, Arthur Mac’s, Satay by the Bay, and Tea on Piedmont, as well as newcomers MOMOlicious, Lahore Di Khushboo, Sunrise Deli, Hila Gelato, and Annie’s T Cakes. With building community a central theme of Food Fest, the organizers will be featuring the Community Zone – a vibrant gathering place for attendees to get to know local organizations such as No Immigrants No Spice, Oakland Promise, Piedmont Language School, Soccer Without Borders, Camp Augusta, Piedmont Asian American Club, League of Women Voters, Linda Beach Cooperative Playschool, and Piedmont Play School. Food Festers are advised to come early to get a good seat and enjoy this year’s performances, which include the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, Oakland Taiko, Beloved Little Circus, O Hina’aro Nui Tahitian Dance & Music, Hiiiwav Black Artist Incubator, Devendra Sharma Folk Opera Ensemble, and Amor do Samba. No Immigrants No Spice will be bringing back their interactive trivia game and audience members will hear from Chef James Yeun Leong Parry from Michelin-rated restaurant Benu and most recently his Chinese pop-up, The Happy Crane. Visit www.piedmontfoodfest. org for more information on this can’t miss community experience. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Potential donors can sign up online or over the phone The American Red Cross will hold a blood drive at Veterans Memorial Hall, 401 Highland Avenue, on Saturday, March 30, from 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The drive is sponsored by the City of Piedmont. Donating blood products is important to community health, according to the Red Cross. Every two seconds someone in the U.S. needs blood and or platelets, but only about 3% of age-eligible people donate each year. Blood donations through the Red Cross are used for patients in need of surgery, cancer treatment, and transfusions for blood loss from traumatic injuries. In addition to traditional blood donation, the Red Cross will also be soliciting “Power Red” donations, a new process where a specialized machine allows donors to safely donate two units of red blood cells during one donation while also returning any plasma and platelets to the donor’s body. This way, donors can give nearly twice the amount of red cells at one time and help more patients. For busy donors looking to maximize their impact on the community, Power Red donations are an effective method. Power red cell donation takes about 20-30 minutes longer than a whole blood donation and you can donate approximately every four months. Donors may select either blood donation or Power Red donation at the time of registration. To register for an appointment, visit http://RedCrossBlood.org or call 1-800-REDCROSS.

articles.text: The Piedmont Fire Department has extended the deadline for its disaster preparedness survey through Sunday, April 14. The survey asks what type of disasters community members are concerned about, what steps they have taken to prepare for a disaster, and what barriers keep community members from becoming better prepared. The survey should take about three minutes to complete, according to the city’s website. Survey responses will help city officials better understand baseline levels of preparedness within the community, where gaps exist, and how they can best support more residents taking important steps to be ready for a disaster. The fire department plans on using these responses to plan future education, outreach efforts, and programming built around emergency preparedness. After the survey is finished, the City of Piedmont will publish the results on its survey website. The survey will remain open through Sunday, April 14, and is available at www.piedmont. ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. For more information about how to prepare your household for emergencies, visit piedmont.ca.gov/disaster. For residents with questions about the preparedness survey, please contact Fire Chief Dave Brannigan at dbrannigan@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Fire Dept. disaster preparedness survey extended to April 14

articles.text: Last week, approximately 200 children searching for eggs took over Piedmont Park during the Recreation Department’s Bunny Blast. On Saturday, March 23, children aged two to eight got to search for over 5000 plastic eggs. The festivities began at 9:45 a.m., with separate hunts scheduled for the four age groups. Other activities for kids included decorating bags in which they could put their eggs, face painting, and photo opportunities with the Easter Bunny in the Community Hall. Each hunt also included three golden eggs that could be turned in at Bunny’s Burrow outside Community Hall for a special gift, adding a sense of mystery and competition to an already lively event. “There was a lot of energy. All our little ones were pretty excited for the egg hunt. I don’t know if The Easter Bunny himself was available for photos inside the Community Hall. controlled chaos would describe it best,” said Akil Danjuma, who organized the event’s egg hunt for the third year in a row. If he could do anything differently, Danjuma stated he would like to hold next year’s event at a larger venue. Danjuma was grateful for the event’s turnout, despite the occasional light rain. “Thank you to the people of Piedmont for supporting our programs. Conditions were less than ideal, but people still came out, weren’t worried about getting wet, and still had fun.” Children participate in an egg hunt in Piedmont Main Park.

articles.text: Ruth Alahydoian, Piedmont School District business manager, delivered the second interim financial report to the school board on March 13. The district’s budget received a “Positive Certification” and the budget is set to meet all financial obligations, including the requirement of 3% reserve. “Funds have been set aside for our offers for employee groups,” said Alahydoian. Highlights of the budget report show that 51% of all revenues come in the form of Local Control Funding (LCFF) which is $26.6 million this year. Another 37%, or $14.2 million is generated locally from PEF, parent donations and parcel taxes. The district gets $22,611 per pupil in revenues. A key topic of discussion in negotiations with the teacher union has been the Cost of Living Adjustment of COLA, which showed an 8.22% increase akin to inflation. Essentially, costs have increased, but PUSD only received a revenue increase to the tune of 8.22% on the LCFF part of revenue, which is only (51%) of all revenue. “The 8.22% ended up being really just a 4% in LCFF dollars, which was about a million dollars increased from last year to this year.” explained Alahydoian. “Next year the projection is for the COLA to be less than 1%, and with continued declining enrollment we will have a decline in our revenue,” she added. The PUSD budget includes almost $800,000 more in revenues up to $52.2 million since the first interim report; expenditures have also increased by $85,000. Recent budget cuts have given the district the flexibility to eliminate a number of teaching positions before next year. Pink slip notices went out to teachers on March 15, giving them advance notice that the district may not have the funds to hire them back for the 2024-25 school year. Savings have also been created by the planned reduction of hours for existing CSEA classified staff members. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, March 27, 2024 17th Annual Summer Camps Edition By Vicky Chen Children’s Fairyland has long been a cherished destination for families, and its Summer Day Camps are no exception. With each passing year, these camps continue to grow in popularity, often selling out well in advance. During our strategic planning process in 2021, we conducted a focus group and older campers who have ‘aged-out’ of the typical camp age range expressed a strong interest in extending their time with our storybook theme Level Up at Fairyland Summer Camp park. In response to this feedback, we’re excited to announce our efforts to make Summer Day Camp even more inclusive and appealing to older children. For the last two summers, we’ve been expanding our offerings to cater to a wider age range, introducing specialty camps like Farm to Table and Fairyland Puppeteers. In Farm to Table, campers ages 5 to 11 delve into a curriculum that focuses on the journey of food from seed to plate, gaining a deeper appreciation for the land and our animal residents along the way. In Fairyland Puppeteers, 8 to 11-year-olds collaborate on crafting and performing their own puppet show, experiencing firsthand the magic of storytelling. From designing and creating their unique puppet characters to scripting and staging their imaginative tales, campers are fully immersed in the creative process, enjoying teamwork and self-expression. These camps not only provide opportunities for older campers to deepen their connection with Fairyland but also ignite campers’ imaginations and instill valuable Kids learn how to plant vegetables in the Farm to Table summer camp at Children’s Fairyland. Children’s Fairyland campers show off their puppeteering skiills at Puppeteer Camp. Campers are taught baking and cooking skills in the Farm to Table Children’s Fairyland Camp. skills that extend beyond the confines of our park. As we evolve the curriculum for our Summer Day Camp, we’re committed to investing more time into crafting tailored themes and activities for 9 to 11-year-old campers, nurturing their independence while allowing their creativity to blossom. The key ingredient to making camp a fun place for all is ensuring that everyone feels like they belong. Each cohort kicks off with community-building activities, including crafting group agreements and exchanging introductions to learn about each other’s names, likes, and dislikes. These activities continue throughout their time together, fostering an environment of caring and sharing. Eleven-year-old Manoah, a seasoned camper, shares his unique perspective on the appeal of Fairyland’s camps: “It never gets repetitive. It’s like a video game that’s infinitely ‘re-playable,’ and you never get tired of it. It’s always fun, but as you get older, the way it’s fun changes.” Manoah’s reflections on his camp experience highlight the dynamic nature of our programs. As we continue to ‘level up’ our offerings, his insight reinforces the importance of creating engaging experiences tailored to older campers in our community. Manoah has been participating in Theatre Camp regularly. “My favorite activity of all time are the ice breakers at the beginning of camp,” said Manoah. “I really like how the counselors mix us up, forcing us to make new friends that we didn’t know before.” Manoah’s fondest memories aren’t tied to specific activities, but rather to the camaraderie fostered during icebreaker sessions – an aspect of Summer Day Camp that encourages friendships to flourish beyond the park’s gates. Manoah will age out of Summer Day Camp and hopefully join our Counselor-in-Training Program (CIT) next summer. Our CIT program allows our veteran campers to continue at Fairyland while practicing leadership skills and helping younger children. As we eagerly prepare for the camp’s opening on June 3, there are still a few openings available for 9 to 11-year-old campers – a rare occurrence at this stage. For those seeking a memorable summer experience, we invite you to join us at Children’s Fairyland Summer Day Camp, where adventure and friendships await. A chartered bus will provide safe passage to and from and will leave Piedmont at 7:00 a.m. on Friday, April 19. The tournament is a fundraiser for Wildwood School and will reward the dads with some recreation after a full calendar of its events, such as the Pumpkin Patch and Crab Feed. This all-inclusive event is prime for anyone looking for a day of fun. After the round of golf the Dads and friends will barbecue some ribs and hot dogs as they share the day’s bloopers, high notes, and adventures. “Oakmoore is the perfect spot to close the year for the dads club,” said event organizer Reed Johnson. “We’ve got a bus from the center of town to make the transportation easy and the whole course to ourselves. articles.text: Dominant wins over Las Lomas, Bishop O’Dowd, College Park Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team is on fire as it enters the final month of their regular season.. The Highlanders are on a three-game winning streak after defeating Las Lomas 10-5 on Tuesday, March 19, an easy 16-3 drubbing of league rival Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, March 22, and an equally dominating 15-5 victory over College Park 15-5 on Monday, March 25. All three matches were played at home. “I think what the team has demonstrated over the last few games is that they can play as a team. It starts with defense in terms of great communication and early slides. On the attack we saw a lot of patience, just waiting for the right shot instead of the first shot. That’s a testament to the team knowing each other a little bit better,” said assistant coach Greg Tschider, who was filling in for coach Carlton Chan who was attending the graduation of his daughter. The victory over Western Alameda County Conference nemesis O’Dowd puts Piedmont in the driver’s seat of the league tournament on April 24-26. However, PHS first has to take care of business with Berkeley tomorrow, Thursday, March 28 at Witter Field. “Knock on wood, we continue to be hopeful in building a strong ranking. Every game we talk about getting five percent better. We’re pleased with how we’ve played so far, but we still believe we haven’t played our best lacrosse,” Tschider said. It’s been a strong offensive performance for the Highlanders with 41 goals over the three victories. Ruby Guzdar continues to lead the team with her speed and shooting accuracy, recording seven goals against O’Dowd, five on College Park and another two against Las Lomas. “I feel like we’re connecting really well as an offense. We have a lot of set plays, but with this game we were just cutting and making connections outside of plays. I feel like we’re very connected this year,” Guzdar said. Friedie Schickedanz is also making a big impact regularly in possession with wrap-around goals and slick assists. “Especially after the O’Dowd game, we’re feeling really good,” said Schickedanz. “At this point, we’ve played most of our games. We want to improve every game and the last two games, we’ve really come in with the mentality that they will be close games. We came out strong and put points on the board.” 15-5 over College Park Piedmont held a comfortable 4-1 lead by the end of the first quarter and extended the gap to 11-2 by halftime. They added three unanswered goals in the third quarter to activate the running clock with around 10 minutes left in the game, then scored one more in the fourth while allowing three. articles.text: Artist’s solo exhibit ends in May Artist Lhola Amira with Philisa: Zinza Mphefumlo Wami (2022) Lhola Amira: Facing the Future will be on display at the de Young Museum in San Francisco through May. The solo exhibition interprets the museum’s African art collection as a living and evolving practice through the lens of contemporary art. “Lhola Amira: Facing the Future” centers art from Africa as a site of critical exploration for the evolving nature of African culture. Lhola Amira, a South African artist, is offering visitors ways of becoming more open and more sensitized to the pain of others, and the possibilities of the present,” said Natasha Becker, curator of African art for the museum. Artworks from de Young’s permanent collection are placed with Amira’s work, exploring the themes of wounding and healing. Selections include African art pieces from the 19th and 20th century art, including sculptures and ceremonial pieces. On view is Philisa: Zinza Mphefumlo Wami (2022), an art portal considering sacred spaces for the cleansing of wounds, honoring ancestors, and fostering connection. Guests are invited to enter this interactive art portal with healing in mind. Also included in the exhibition is the single-channel video projection IRMANDADE: The Shape of Water in Pindorama (2018–2020), produced by Amira in Bahia, Brazil. To learn more, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/lhola-amira.
articles.title: Last chance to see Lhola Amira: Facing the Future at de Young

articles.text: An exhibition featuring new work by UC Berkeley Professor Emeritus of Arts Mary Lovelace O’Neal is now on view at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA). O’Neal, whose work spans six decades, focuses on abstracted mixed-media and minimalism using black as a backdrop. Her earliest works used “lampblack pigment,” or powdered soot created from burning oil. The strong, dark background provides a foundation for vibrant hues of paint, glitter and other materials she uses over it. “Painting with color was always a surprise. [It was] like dancing with the paint,” she said. O’Neal often explores themes of social justice, social movements, music and literature in her paintings. She was hired at the University of California, Berkeley in 1979, where she became the first African American professor awarded tenure in the Department of Art in 1985, chair of the department in 1999, and professor emerita in 2006. To learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/new-work-mary-lovelaceoneal/. La Pieta (2021-23) by Mary Lovelace O’Neal

articles.text: Entry deadline is April 15 Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside has announced its annual haiku contest is currently underway. Interested participants may submit entries by Monday, April 15. Submit up to three original haiku poems in the traditional haiku format of three short lines of five, seven, and five syllables. Submissions in languages other than English are strongly encouraged as long as they follow haiku poem-structure. This year’s contest theme is migration and belonging. Filoli is San Mateo Poet Laureate Aileen Cassinetto looking for poems that muse on how beings create a sense of home in gardens and the natural world, and encourages content based on its spring blooms. The winner will receive the Ecopoetry Award, which celebrates this theme while touching on the connection between humans and the environment. The second place winner will receive a Filoli individual membership. The poems will be judged by former San Mateo Poet Laureate Aileen Cassinetto. The ten semi-finalist poems will be announced on Filoli’s website on Earth Day, April 22. Prize winners will be announced May 1. For more information, visit https://filoli.org/haiku/.
articles.title: Filoli House and Garden plans annual Spring haiku contest

articles.text: A solo show of paintings by Carolyn Lord will open at Piedmont Center of the Arts on April 6 and will feature paintings inspired by Googie architecture, flower gardens, and the California landscape. There will also be a group of landscapes inspired by a trip to Colorado. Lord is best known for her watercolors with sophisticated color and bold compositions, influenced by the California Watercolor Style of artists such as Millard Sheets and George Post. She has been active in the Oakland arts community for many years, recently as a full-time student at the Golden Gate Atelier. She has participated in plein air events in Sonoma and Crested Butte, Colorado and has had paintings in juried shows at the Triton Salon, De Young Open, and Greater Bay Area Open. For detailed information about galleries that represent her work, in Santa Rosa, San Francisco, and Carmel; and upcoming watercolor workshops in Denver, Berkeley, and Whidbey Island, see: www.carolynlord.com Open Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays on April 6-7, 13-14, and April 20-21. An opening reception will be held on April 6 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Informal drawing and painting demonstration will take place on April 13-14. A closing reception is scheduled on April 21 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.

articles.text: Performances at ODC Theatre in SF on April 5 & 6 Oakland Ballet’s third annual Dancing Moons Festival ends next week with performances on April 5 and 6 at the ODC Theatre in San Francisco. The program is choreographed by all-Asian American Pacific Islander talent and will include a preview of the dance company’s Angel Island Project with choreography by Natasha Adorlee and Feng Ye. The project took inspiration from poetry carved by detainees at the Angel Island Immigration Station. The station held thousands of immigrants from 1910 through 1940, mainly from China, Japan, India and the Philippines. “With captured imaginations, we take on a flight of discovery and storytelling shaped by a beautiful score by Chinese American composer Huang Ruo, and the inspired poetry that was carved in the walls by detainees,” Oakland Ballet Artistic Director Graham Lustig said. “The Angel Island Project helps us to trace who we are today by remembering from where we came.” Several selections will also be presented at the festival as works in progress, including Layer Upon Layer by Caili Quan (2022), Ballet des Porcelaines or The Teapot Prince by Phil Chan (original 1739; reimagined 2021), and highlights of Exquisite Corpse by Elaine Kudo, Seyong Kim, and Phil Chan (2023). For the first time since the festival’s inception, an exhibition of visual artists will be displayed at the cultural center. Artists include Asian Americans Sanjay Vora, Mark Shigenga and JaYing Wang. To purchase tickets, visit https://oaklandballet.org/dancing-moons-festival/.

articles.text: A scene from the 2024 Academy Award winner for Best Documentary, 20 Days in Mariupol In late February of 2022, Vladimir Putin announced to the world that Russia, for reasons of “self defense,” would begin a “special military operation” into Ukraine. Putin had barely finished his stated rationale for the unprovoked invasion when the industrial port city of Mariupol, 35 miles from the Russian border, saw troops and large tanks bearing the white letter Z begin arriving for what would be the first of countless assaults on Ukraine. Homes, apartment buildings, hospitals (to include a maternity hospital) were shelled and defenseless civilians wounded or killed. Many fled the country, while others remained in their homes or apartment buildings. Many hid in basements or took refuge where they could. Trapped in the now besieged city (a single corridor out of Mariupol was soon closed) was a small team of Ukrainian video journalists, led by Mstyslav Chernov. Realizing what seemed about to unfold, they made the existential choice to remain in the city at their peril, and commit to documenting with their available video gear the first 20 days of what we know now devolved into a relentless and brutal war. At the time, director/photographer Chernov had no way of knowing that all they would witness and film and experience in those bleak days was mere prologue to what awaited the Ukrainian people. Winner of an Academy Award for Best Documentary, 20 Days in Mariupol is an extraordinary story, narrated by Chernov in what at times seems a stunned whisper as if the destruction and carnage inflicted on the innocent was more than he can bear. Yet, knowing that he and his small crew were at great risk – at one point he acknowledges what would be a grim fate if they were captured – he insists that somehow they must get the recorded footage out to a waiting Associated Press contact as well as the world. Those dispatches are what comprise this emotionally immersive film. At one point the journalists seek safe shelter at what is referred to as hospital number two where severely wounded and dying civilians are arriving in such numbers that the surgeries, rooms, and hallways are overwhelmed. The morgue is soon filled, and bodies are now taken to the basement to await not funerals but simply burial. At the insistence of the doctors and nurses, some crying, Chernov films a severely wounded 4-year-old girl, her frantic mother desperate and shattered. With little medical supplies available, a medical emergency team tries to save her and fails. A 16-year-old boy arrives. He had been playing soccer on a nearby field when an artillery shell struck and his legs were blown off. His father holds him, weeping, grief palpable, unable to accept that his son is dead. Later, we see images of a long trench and watch as lifeless, anonymous bodies – men, women, and children – are laid not to rest but are soon covered with a blanket of soil. It is agonizing and soul piercing to see revealed Russia’s intended consequences. Clearly, the war that we see is one aimed at civilians, and the dispatches from which this documentary is created put the lie to any disinformation claiming that is anything else. 20 Days in Mariupol has been recognized worldwide as a superb, courageous film. It won a Pulitzer Prize; an Oscar for Best International Feature Film; a Directors Guild of America award; and was named one of the top five documentary films of 2023. At the Sundance Film Festival it was selected for the Audience Award. Put simply, it is a remarkable tableau that is both unflinching and unforgettable. 20 Days in Mariupol. Documentary. Directed by Mstyslav Chernov. Produced by Frontline and PBS. 1 hr., 34 min. Released in 2023. Streaming on VUDU/ prime/apple tv.

articles.text: There are many reasons to watch Barney’s Version. Foremost would be Paul Giamatti who delivers one of his best performances since the memorable Sideways (a must-see). Giamatti is the antithesis of a Hollywood leading man. He is short, paunchy, his appearance unkempt, his hairline heading south. But what Giamatti can do is act. He can inhabit a character with passion and commitment, his face and eyes (a bit large and protruding) and slouching posture conveying complex and contradictory emotions. In Barney’s Version, he portrays Barney Panofsky, an aging producer of a daytime television soap. He’s hugely flawed, has had three wives, is self-absorbed, drinks too much whiskey, ignores those who love him for hockey, and smokes too many cigars. He’s also smart, impulsive, attractive in a strange off-putting way, generous and selfish almost simultaneously. And, indeed, his father, Izzy – played sublimely by Dustin Hoffman – is unwavering in his love of Barney and blessed with a sense of humor. You’ve seen Hoffman smile as only he can. Everything about this film is bittersweet. Funny and sad and wonderful. Based on a novel by Mordecai Richler, Barney’s Version is an intriguing character study of a picaresque man who, for example, on the eve of his wedding to his second wife, spots a stunning woman across the room and falls in love. Her name is Miriam, she lives in New York (the film is set in Montreal), and she is leaving on a train to return home. Barney abandons everyone at the reception and rushes to the train station, fully prepared to change his life instantly if she will consider going away with him. She asks him if he hasn’t lost his mind. A relevant question. But in Barney’s version of his life, his actions make all the sense in the world. Miriam is played by the stunning Rosamund Pike, and she and Giamatti share moments on screen that are magical. But then, the film is replete with fine performances to include Mini Driver as wife number two and Scott Speedman as a gifted Bohemian drug-addicted writer. At the center of this film, in every frame, is Giamatti, who won a Golden Globe for his portrayal of Barney. Why he was not nominated for an Oscar is inexplicable. Barney’s Version. Directed by Richard L. Lewis. Starring Paul Giamatti, Dustin Hoffman, Rosamund Pike, Minnie Driver, Scott Speedman and Rachel Lefevre. 2 hrs., 12 min. Rated R. Released 2011. articles.text: Being a triple threat is one of the miracles of sports. Baseball had Willie Mays, and now Shohei Ohtani. In basketball, there is Stephen Curry. How does this apply in music? Well, this is a different story. Famed sports commentator Howard Cosell boasted that he “never played the game.“ He sure missed a lot. It’s fun to participate. Good amateur orchestras abound. Let’s have a look behind the scenes. First, you need the musicians – competence is important. So is organization. The third element is to have a good director. In classical music, the conductor is the star of the show. But what makes a good conductor? It’s not just waving your arms and making “sacrifices at the altar of music.” The conductor is the unifying force as well as the inspirational leader of the players. articles.text: One of your important sources of retirement income will likely be Social Security — but when should you start taking it? You can start collecting Social Security benefits at 62, but your checks will be considerably bigger if you wait until your full retirement age, which is likely between 66 and 67. You could even wait until you’re 70, at which point the payments will max out, except for yearly cost-of-living adjustments. But if you need the money, you need the money, even if you’re just 62 or any age before full retirement age. However, if you have adequate financial resources to meet your monthly needs, whether through earned income, your investment portfolio or a combination of the two, you could have some flexibility in choosing when to take Social Security. In this case, you may want to weigh these considerations: • Life expectancy – For all of us, it’s one of life’s great mysteries: How long will we live? Of course, we can’t see into the future, so the question can’t be answered with total confidence. But to make an informed decision on when to take Social Security, you don’t need to know your exact lifespan — you just need to make a reasonably good estimate. So, for example, if you’re approaching 62, you’re enjoying excellent health and you have a family history of longevity, you might conclude it’s worth waiting a few years to collect Social Security, so you can receive the bigger payments. Conversely, if your health is questionable and your family has not been fortunate in terms of longevity, you might want to start taking your benefits earlier. • Employment – You can certainly continue working and still receive Social Security benefits. However, if you’re under your full retirement age for the entire year, Social Security will deduct $1 from your benefits for every $2 you earn above the annual limit of $22,320. In the year you reach your full retirement age, Social Security will deduct $1 in benefits for every $3 you earn above $59,520. So, you may want to keep these reductions in mind when deciding when to begin accepting benefits. Once you reach your full retirement age, you can earn any amount without losing benefits. (Also, at your full retirement age, Social Security will recalculate your benefit amount to credit you for the months you received reduced benefits because of your excess earnings.) • Spouse – Spouses can receive two types of Social Security benefits: spousal and survivor. With a spousal benefit, your spouse can receive up to 50% of your full retirement benefits, regardless of when you start taking them. (Your spouse’s benefit can be reduced by the amount of their own retirement benefit and whether they took Social Security before their full retirement age.) But with a survivor benefit, your decision about when to take Social Security can make a big difference. A surviving spouse can receive the larger of their own benefit or 100% of a deceased spouse’s benefit, so if you take benefits early and receive a permanent reduction, your spouse’s survivor benefit may also be reduced for their lifetime. When to take Social Security is an important and irrevocable decision. So, consider all the factors before making your choice. articles.text: Garden column by Josh Harkinson I must admit, I’ve always been biased against hydrangeas. In Greek mythology, the hydra is a serpent-like water monster with nine heads. In California ecology, it is a non-native that requires too much irrigation. But oh, how it charms you. Large emerald-green leaves. Delicate baby-blue flowers mounded together like pompoms at a pep rally. Sweet perfume wafting through the summer shade. A few months ago, I got a letter from a reader asking how to cultivate this devilish beauty. I didn’t respond for a long time, but a seed had been planted. I started thinking about a section of my split-rail fence along the street where the natives had died for lack of sun and a blackberry bramble had run amok. I wanted a shade-tolerant, flowering hedge that would be four to six feet tall. I went to Ace Garden Center and asked about the Hydrangea Nikko Blue in five-gallon pots ($39.99 each). The manager said it needed water once a week, which seemed reasonable enough. I came home with three of them. I wish I could say things have gone well since then. This simple purchase has unleashed a can of worms—or, you might say, a multi-headed snake monster. Surveying my hydrangea plot, I realized that I should first cut down the nearby, 30-foot tall pittosporum that has been turning what would be a shady spot into deep shade. Pittosporum is what real estate agents plant when they want to gussy up a housing flip. They start off as relatively attractive, low-maintenance, fast-growing shrubs, but quickly get out of control if left to their own devices. I inherited one a decade ago that I wish I’d cut out sooner. Thus began a frenzy of tree trimming. I filled up three compost bins with pittosporum branches and amassed many more in a pile. If I’d planted the hydranMy new hydrangeas, with the remnants of the pittosporum in the background. geas first, the falling branches would have crushed them. Next, I set about digging out the dead ceonothus bushes on the fence line along with the berry brambles covering them. I couldn’t figure out why I was having so much trouble removing a particular stump, until my shovel pierced an underground PVC irrigation line and unleashed a geyser—a water monster if I’ve ever seen one. “How did you make that rainbow?” asked my daughter, looking up from the spot at a nearby table where she’d been doing her homework. Needless to say, I haven’t gotten around to planting the hydrangeas yet. When I do, I will make sure they have moist, welldrained soil with lots of organic matter. If you have heavy clay soil you can also add a bit of sand. The same hydrangea plant will yield differently colored flowers depending upon the soil. At a PH of less than 7, the plant will readily take up aluminum, causing it to produce blue flowers. At a higher PH, the flowers will be pink. You can raise the soil PH by adding lime and lower it by adding sulfur and sphagnum moss. Whatever you do, go in prepared! For every problem you chop off, two more can grow back. Journalist and ardent gardener Josh Harkinson lives along a creek near Piedmont Avenue with two kids, four chickens, and a wife who thinks he spends too much time gardening.

articles.text: Part 1 In Northern California, we live in wine heaven. We are surrounded by incredible wine regions like Napa, Sonoma and the Santa Cruz Mountains. Yet, one of the highlights of my year is my annual trip abroad to taste wines from one of the world’s great wine regions. Every year I team up with my wine-loving colleagues Richard Wing and Terry Hershey to visit an iconic wine region. Over the years we have tasted wine in Portugal, Spain, Bordeaux, Languedoc, Rhone Valley and Italy. This year, we set our sights on two very different French wine regions – Burgundy and Bandol – and tackled them both in ten days. (Read more on Bandol in the weeks ahead.) Burgundy battles Bordeaux for the title of France’s greatest wine region, but the two could not be more different. Bordeaux is the land of Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot and huge, impressive chateaus and estates. Burgundy is the land of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay grown by hundreds of small producers making tiny amounts of wine. The Cote d’Or which stretches from just south of Dijon to ten miles south of Beaune is a small region divided into thousands of tiny vineyard plots called climats. International demand for the wines and the small amounts produced have caused the price of Burgundy wine to skyrocket. The world’s most expensive wine, Domaine Romanee-Conti Romanee-Conti, now sells for $16,000 a bottle for the current vintage. It is said the land it grows on is the most expensive property in the world. We had the pleasure of visiting eight different Burgundy wine estates from large negociants to small family farmers. Here is part one of my report. of Volnay, they have roots in winemaking dating back to the 16th century. Directed today by Etienne Montille, who has expanded the estates’ holdings to 35 hectares – very large for Burgundy – Montille has not limited his focus to Burgundy and has established wine projects in California and Japan. They have vineyards in most of the important appellations – Beaune, Volnay, Pommard, Corton Clos Vogeout, Vosne-Romanee, Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet. I was able to taste through the 2022 vintage which will be arriving in the U.S. soon. 2022 was a wonderful vintage especially in contrast to 2021, when the weather caused many crop failures. The wines we tasted were uniformly and beautifully crafted with great balance and structure and a sure sense of terroir. Check availability at orders@beauneimports.com. FAVORITE WINE • 2022 Domaine de Montille Pommard 1st Cru les Rugiens The Pommard les Rugiens unwinds in the glass to reveal an enchanting nose of dark berry fruit mingled with anise, orange rind, warm spices, loamy soil and deep bass notes. Full-bodied, velvety, and concentrated, it’s a deep, seamless, profound wine that’s the most muscular and potentially long-lived cuvee in the range. articles.text: Beate Illek, a former Piedmont resident, spoke to representatives of the California Congressional delegation on March 19 about priority issues affecting 40 million Americans who experience headache disorders and migraine disease. “It is important for our Congressmen and Congresswomen to realize that one of four households in America have a member living with migraine”, said Dr. Illek. Dr. Illek represented California along with 275 other Alliance for Headache Disorders Advocacy (AHDA) advocates from all 50 states as part of the AHDA’s annual Headache on the Hill advocacy day. Dr. Illek met with the Congressional staff of Sen. Laphonza Butler, as well as Rep. Barbara Lee and Representative Scott Peters. This marked the return of the first fully in-person Headache on the Hill (HOH) since before the pandemic. Senators and Congress members were encouraged to co-sponsor the Safe Step Act. “Step therapy, sometimes called a ‘fail-first requirement,’ is a protocol in which a health insurer will deny coverage for a prescribed prescription or treatment until an alternative insurer-preferred treatment is first attempted,” explained Illek. Patients with headache disorders are some of the most impacted by step therapy protocols and are often required to try at least three medications before getting the treatment their provider originally recommended. Legislators were also asked to consider cosponsoring the NIH Clinical Trial Diversity Act which seeks to address critical gaps in clinical research by promoting inclusivity and diversity in clinical trials. The Act underscores the necessity of including a broad spectrum of participants to ensure that scientific advancements benefit all communities equally. Dr. Illek also advocated for robust funding for the Veterans Health Administration’s Headache Disorders Centers of Excellence. Headache disorders are prevalent in the veteran population and 92% of military personnel with mild traumatic brain injury experience post-traumatic headaches. Headache disorder centers of excellence are charged with improving headache care quality, delivery, and access for Veterans living with headaches. They also prioritize training and research. As of fiscal year 2023, more than 1.99 million Veterans received headache care across more than 12.6 million visits for headache within VA Medical Centers and the need is far greater that the current Centers can support. The 2024 Headache on the Hill event in Washington DC was represented by 275 advocates from all 50 states this year.

articles.text: Participating with the Walking on Wednesdays group last week were Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Alan Goldhammer, Chuck Oraftik, Jim Kuo, Renee Goldhammer, Irene Thompson, Jim Kellogg, Elizabeth Richter, Martin Levy, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Alicia Rivera, Swee Ling Chen, Peggy Shultz, Gloria DaSilva, Melba Yee, Adrienne Hamlin, Karin Fetherston, Priscilla Wanerus, Larry Olsen, Jack Fischrup, Claudine Bach, Joanne Larson, Sharona Fischrup, Charlene Louie, Helene Farber, Nancy Olsen, Edith Lee, Phil Witte, Sherry Jacobs, Brenda Ferrero, Marianne Jakus, Bill Ahern, Joyce Ahern, Shirley Nakao, Lisa Euphrat, Leigh Sorensen with K-9 best friend McDuff, and Dick Carter. The Walking on Wednesdays’ group had a solid turnout of 37 walkers and two K-9 best friends last week, with a destination of the Glen Alpine-Sotelo loop. On the way, they passed large Easter egg displays on Highland and Sheridan and stopped in front of 395 Hampton Road at the foot of Glen Alpine. The home, formally known as Hampton House, had been on the real estate market and is listed as an eight bedroom/9 bath, 11,870 square foot home on 1+ acres with space for eight cars. It was listed for $14.5 million. Gail Lombardi, President of the Piedmont Historical Society, provided some background. Albert Farr, who designed City Hall and Piedmont Community Church, designed this elegant Mediterranean home in 1927. Tall windows, a Spanish tile roof, shutters and a symmetrical façade complete his design. Farr designed this home for William St. Cyr Cavalier and his wife Camille in 1926. Cavalier was an investment broker and president of his own business, William Cavalier & Company. The Cavaliers had three children when they built this home, and a nurse and servant to help. Cavalier ultimately merged his company with Dean Witter and Co. He died in 1945, but Camille continued to live in the house until her death in 1966. Several new owners have remodeled it, but it continues to maintain Farr’s grand design. Farr has been called one of the most artistic architects on the West Coast. He practiced from 1905 to 1937 and designed more than 40 homes in Piedmont. There was more history too. Before Hampton House was built, Louis Titus, a successful Berkeley real estate developer, bought 50 acres in the Piedmont hills in 1911. He intended to build a Spanish-Italian mansion to be called “Greenacres.” However, in 1912 the Piedmont’s Board of Trustees, now called the City Council, decided new property taxes were needed to pay for the new City’s public services. They passed taxes based on the amount of land owned, and Titus’ taxes were increased to a reported $200,000. He decided Piedmont was not such a great place for this mansion. Greenacres was never built. Next was the story of James Tyson, a wealthy lumber and shipping businessman. In 1914, he purchased 30 acres from Titus’ tract to build his estate, “Oakmont,” at what is now 70 Sotelo. It was listed for $14.5 million. Gail Lombardi, President of the Piedmont Historical Society, provided some background. Albert Farr, who designed City Hall and Piedmont Community Church, designed this elegant Mediterranean home in 1927. Tall windows, a Spanish tile roof, shutters and a symmetrical façade complete his design. Farr designed this home for William St. Cyr Cavalier and his wife Camille in 1926. Cavalier was an investment broker and president of his own business, William Cavalier & Company. The Cavaliers had three children when they built this home, and a nurse and servant to help. Cavalier ultimately merged his company with Dean Witter and Co. He died in 1945, but Camille continued to live in the house until her death in 1966. Attendees were also encouraged to enjoy the thousands of tulips in bloom around the cemetery grounds, planted during December in time for them to bloom at the In the hour before the exhibit opened ,florists scurried across the chapel floor, adjusting their design pieces with meticulous focus. Because each artist is working with tulips, which wilt throughout the day, each exhibit requires a small amount of maintenance each morning to remain fresh. “Tulips tend to drink a lot of water,” said florist Suzy Skram as she changed the water in her exhibit’s pot. “They need a lot of encouragement to keep looking beautiful. Adding fresh water daily and even cutting the stems will encourage the tulips to last throughout the show.” Florist Susan Cohn said that although creating art with tulips was difficult, she liked the meaning it brought to each piece. “Just like life, the tulips are transitory. They’re not here forever,” she explained. A few florists also took time to speculate why the event has so much staying power with audiences year after year. “Flowers tell a story,” said florist Francesca Ricci. “You can ask women what flowers they had for a graduation corsage or something specific that they wanted in a wedding bouquet or something incredibly beautiful that someone gave them at some time. Piedmont Real Estate Update March 2024 Generational Trends in Real Estate We often hear about the impact Millennials have had on the world since they came of age decades ago. From dominating the workplace and shaping social media to being environmentally conscious and native to the world of technology, they have undeniably altered the landscape. Their effect on real estate has also had an impact. From 2014 - 2022, Millennials formed the biggest share of buyers. However, in 2023, many home buyers of that generation put off a purchase due to the high cost of borrowing and unique buying habits. As a result, Gen Xers and younger Baby Boomers stepped up and took the lead. 2023 Profile of Home Buyers Since 2013, the National Association of Realtors has produced an annual report on the habits and trends of Buyers and Sellers. In 2023, we saw a few interesting data points in their research that we wanted to share. “Seventy-eight percent of home buyers financed their home purchase—a share that decreases as the age of the buyer increases. Younger buyers continue to depend on savings for their downpayment, while older buyers use proceeds from the sale of their previous residence. Twentytwo percent of younger Millennials received downpayment help in the form of a gift or a loan from a friend or relative. Older Millennial and Gen X buyers’ purchases were delayed the longest due to debt at a median of five years. Buyers overall were delayed primarily by student loan debt and high rental costs holding back saving. In fact, 35 percent of younger Millennials reported having student loan debt with a median loan balance of $30,000, compared to 30 percent of older Millennials with a median of $40,000. While only three percent of older Boomers had student loan debt with a median balance of $9,000. This may be due to not only their personal educational loans but accumulating debt from their children’s education. * AGE OF HOME BUYERS & SELLERS* Silent Generation 1925 - 1945 Younger Boomers 1955 - 1964 Older Gen Y/ Millennials 1980 - 1989 Gen Z 1999 - 2004 Older Boomers 1946 - 1954 Gen X 1965 - 1979 Younger Gen Y/ Millennnials 1990 - 1998 Characteristics of Home Buyers in 2023* First-time buyers made up 26 percent of all home buyers, a decrease from 34 percent last year.
